## Assigned Readings

📖 Article

- Title: **Ten Simple Rules for the Open Development of Scientific Software**
- Author(s): Andreas Prlić, and James B. Procter
- Year: 2012
- Journal: PLOS Computational Biology
- <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002802>


📖 Article

- Title: **Ten simple rules for documenting scientific software**
- Author(s): Benjamin D. Lee
- Year: 2018
- Journal: PLOS Computational Biology
- <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006561>



## Reflections

::: {.callout-note title="bCourses Submission"}
Submit your answers---to the following questions---to the corresponding 
assignment in bCourses.

Accepted formats: PDF, HTML, MS Word (`.docx`), or Google Doc
:::


## Reflection 1

Locate a function or script you wrote earlier this semester that 
contains line-by-line inline comments.

- Quote a comment you wrote that simply restated what the syntax was doing 
(e.g., `# filter out NA values`), and rewrite it to document why that 
step was scientifically or logically necessary for your analysis pipeline.

- Lee emphasizes documenting high-level architecture over inline commentary.
How does looking at your code architecture at a macro level reveal redundancies 
that inline comments masked?


## Reflection 2

Open a code script or computational notebook you wrote more than 3 
months ago (from a prior class or early project). Without running any 
code cells, read through it from top to bottom.

- Record the exact minute mark where you lost context or could no longer 
immediately explain why a specific data transformation, magic number, or 
parameter choice was made.

- Based on Lee's rules for scientific documentation and Prlić & Procter's 
rules for software licensing/open design, list the top three concrete 
modifications you would need to make to this repository today so that 
a completely independent researcher could reproduce your exact analytical 
output without emailing you.


## Reflection 3

Find a script you wrote in the past where you originally wrote zero comments 
because you thought it was "self-explanatory" or simply because you didn't
know about the importance of good comments.

Read that script as if you were a new collaborator joining the project. 
Write formal comments or docstring or file-header for that script detailing: 

a) Explicit input data file or data types and required data structures,

b) Expected output types and missing-value handling, and 

c) Any hidden side effects (e.g., writing files to disk, 
altering global state, or mutating input dataframes). 

d) What critical operational details did the code alone fail to convey?


## Rubric

::: {.callout-important}
Generic responses that do not mention a specific 
past assignment name or unique piece of code from your own experience will 
receive a score of zero.
:::

- **Full Credit (5 Points)**: Response is highly specific, names unique personal 
or localized constraints, and explicitly connects the personal experience 
back to the prompt in each question. Clearly written by a human.

- **Partial Credit (2-3 Points)**: Response is correct but uses vague or generic 
examples (e.g., "I lost a file once" instead of naming the script). Sounds like 
a generic summary an AI could have written.

- **No Credit (0 Points)**: Response relies entirely on abstract definitions, 
fails to provide personal context, or uses copy-pasted text from a webpage
or AI tool.
